On Monday, June 29, 2020 at 5:18:37 PM UTC+1, John Clare wrote:
> Hi Zoe,
>
> You could use the delta method. Just to re-use some dummy code posted elsewhere, to get an estimate of Var(N-hat), you could try something like:
>
> library(emdbook)
> Var_hat<-deltavar(sum(exp(b0+b1*Forest)),
>                          meanval=c(b0=estimateb0, b1=estimateb1),
>                           Sigma=[variance and covariance for b0, b1])
> SE<-sqrt(Var_hat)
>
> Above, assume 'Forest' is a pixel level covariate, so a vector of length nPixels--you'd have to change the beta arguments, lengths, etc. as needed. The variance covariance matrix can be grabbed from the fitted model.
>
> There are a couple of options for constructing the CI. Maybe a lognormal approach makes the most sense. Something like dropping the exp in the deltavar call, and exponentiating log[LCI, UCI]--should be able find some formal descriptions around.
>
> I guess you could also use monte carlo simulation based on the predicted pixel values and estimated variance, although I don't know that there would be any substantive advantage to doing so.
>
> The approaches above focus on expected abundance (a lambda_i rather than the latent N_i), but if you've only sampled a small number of the cells you are trying to predict across, the difference in the CI shouldn't be substantial.
>
> John
> On Friday, June 26, 2020 at 8:17:40 AM UTC-6 Zoe wrote:
> >
> > Hello all,
> >
> >
> > I’m using gdistsamp to estimate abundance. I've used predict to get abundance estimates for a large number of fine scale pixels. I've taken the estimate of the total population size to be the sum of the predicted value for all pixels and I'm now trying to calculate a confidence interval for this value. I've tried to use parboot for this but due to the large number of pixels it’s going to take weeks to run.
> >
> >
> > Is there a way I can calculate a confidence interval manually or will I need to increase my pixel size (i.e. reduce the number of pixels) until parboot will run in a reasonable timeframe?
> >
> >
> > We’re concerned that simply adding up the lower and upper predicted values for all pixels might unduly inflate the CIs because it assumes positive covariance among pixels. We’d like to use something like the delta method, assuming there is no covariance among pixels.
> >
> >
> > I’ve tried taking the square root of the sum of the squared SEs for all pixels, multiplying by 1.96 and adding to/subtracting from the total population estimate to get a 95% CI. I did this on the log scale since that’s what the model uses for abundance, but I end up with “Inf” when I try to back transform the resulting values so clearly that’s not quite right.
> >
> >
> > Any advice would be much appreciated.
> >
> >
> > Many thanks,
> >
> >
> > Zoe

messages.subject_clean: Model SEs compared to bootstrapped SEs too large - stacked years approach
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

My question concerns the bootstrapping that is done after using the stacked years approach (where site/years = sites). There was an earlier thread about this approach (https://groups.google.com/g/unmarked/c/OHkk98y09Zo).

When I took this approach and looked at the ratio of the standard error from the model (SE) to the standard error from the bootstrap (SE.bs) - and the same for the confidence interval length (cil/cil.bs <http://cil.bs>) - , my ratios for this for some parameters were >100 (a couple were in the 200s).

I am using the code provided in the chapter proof from the AHM book as a guide (thanks to Andy Royle for this!), and in that example code, none of the ratios were >100.

Does anyone have any idea what might be going on, or if this is OK? It seems to mean that my SEs and CILs from my original model are much larger than from the bootstrap (at least for some parameters). It seems like this is the opposite of what should happen, since the idea with stacked data is that it might understate the uncertainty, hence the reason for the bootstrap.

Background: I'm using a compilation of different citizen science datasets over a very large area (~90k km2) which I've split into 1 km2 grid cells as different "sites". It's a bit of a trick to get the data to comply with occupancy modeling assumptions because of how it was collected - and that reduced the data available. Could the small amount of data in relation to the large area be what is causing the problem? Or perhaps I'm just missing something more obvious?

Thank you so much for your help!!
Autumn

messages.body_plain:
I think that without the actual data and code one wouldn't be able to pin down the issue.

However, using the site as the bootstrap unit of replication keeps the likely positive correlation among years at a site resulting in smaller standard errors.  (Yes, that's stated a bit loosely).  Now here's an analogy that's maybe even looser:  Suppose you have paired data that would typically be used in a paired t-test.  But for some reason you want to ignore the pairing and perform a two-sample t-test.  But to your rescue is the bootstrap selecting the pair as the bootstrap unit of replication.  Doing so gets you back to the smaller standard errors associated with the paired t-test.

Jim

Hi all, I have not found any other posts about this topic as I doubt it occurs often.

I have presence absence data from a three year period in the early 90s, and then single seasons in 2007 and 2014. The sampling methods were significantly different between the 90s and the 2007/2014 data which resulted in a higher detection rate for the early period (45 min vs 10 min surveys).

My colext analysis runs well for the 90s period. My occu analysis runs well for the 2007 data. The 2014 data is where I am getting hung up.

The issue I have is that this species has experienced tremendous declines in the study area and this species is also difficult to detect. Other published studies have detection ~.3; my 90s data was higher and 2007 data was lower than that.

During the 2014 season, we had 8 detentions from ~500 surveys at 181 points. Every single detection was the only detection at that point.

Obviously, this creates problems in a single season occupancy model when you want to find detection rate. I have tried to use starting values that i acquired from the 2007 single season analysis, but I still get unreasonable occupancy estimates (~1).

My current solution is to run the 2007-2014 data as multi season through colext. I dont know if that is exactly the best solution but it does give more reasonable results.

My primary question is whether there is anything else I can do to force a detection rate into a single season model.

My secondary question is whether there might be another solution to my problem I have yet to think of.

Thank you for the help in advance,

Chance

Getting occupancy estimates of 1 is a "feature" of using maximum likelihood (especially with single detections - there's a formula that tells you when the maximum likelihood estimate is exactly 1).  Using a Bayesian approach will (generally) avoid getting estimates of 1 but that doesn't necessarily mean getting a value that is "reasonable".

I think the colext approach is your best bet in which I assume you're using the same detection function for 2007 and 2014 (and that assumes you're comfortable with that assumption - maybe same crew, same training, same survey protocol).

Jim Baldwin

messages.body_plain:
Hi everybody, I hope this finds you safe and well.

I would like to ask those who have already run multi-season models (function colex()) if you followed any specific procedure. I haven't found any orientation about the steps of model selection using multi-season models except for one in which Marc runs the global model for the four parameters (psi, gamma, epsilon, p) and then does a backward elimination. I'm worried about having an overparameterized model if I do it this way. Because I have 120 sampling points, six covariates for psi, gamma and epsilon, and five for p.

I was thinking about selecting the best covariate for p first, fixing psi as Global, gamma(.) and epsilon(.). Then, select the best covariate for gamma with psi(Global)epsilon(.)p(.). Followed by, a selection of the best covariate for epsilon with psi(Global)gamma(.)p(.). After choosing the best covariates for p, gamma and epsilon, I would fix them with those covariates and vary psi to select the best covariates for it. However, I don't know If it is ok to run this way and if I should do it separately (four steps) or everything together in the same model set.

If anyone has any reference about how to run multi-season models, what are the steps, I would be very thankful.

Thank you so much.

Kind regards.

Att.

Msc. Roberta Montanheiro Paolino
PhD student in Applied Ecology
Conservation and Ecology Lab of Ribeirão Preto (LAEC) - FFCLRP/USP
Wildlife Ecology, Management and Conservation Lab (LEMaC) - ESALQ/USP

John shared a really good paper discussing different modeling strategies and how they impact your inferences. A must-read.

messages.subject: Is model averaging bad?
messages.subject_clean: Is model averaging bad?
messages.body_plain:
Hello unmarked users.

I'm looking for a conversation on the topic of evaluating individual variables across a model set, and didn't really see it in this group, but please let me know if you've seen these questions discussed elsewhere.

Averaging coefficients across models using AIC weights (Burnham and Anderson 02) was (is?) a primary method for evaluating the importance of a variable in a model set..  Brian Cade in a 2015 Ecology paper says this and a couple of other methods are flawed and should be discontinued.  There are rebuttals online, but I don't think any of them were actually published.  On the other hand I found little in the way of additional studies that support Cade's assertions--mainly authors citing Cade, but not showing similar problems through different data.  I am wondering if there is any kind of consensus that Cade is correct and that model averaging is usually flat-out wrong, or if the issue is more nuanced.

So my questions: Is model averaging effective for evaluating the relationship between a variable and a response across a model set in unmarked (e.g., n-mixture models)?  Are there situations where it is acceptable?  What are alternatives for models in unmarked?

A sub-question: is it acceptable to make model-averaged predictions?  I'm uncertain why this would be okay while averaging coefficients would not be okay, so confirmation of that would be helpful.

-Mike Worland

The difference between the two relate to dynamics parameters that describe how N's in time 1 relate to the N's in time 2. Of the two, I'd probably use gdistsamp with the data in hand, but you'd want to have some more formal justification for choosing one.

I'm sure somebody else can give the phiformula question a better response than I can at this moment (and the parameter is explained well in the describing paper, so again, definitely give that a read), but maybe here's a very coarse description. If you visit some soy field on monday and then again on wednesday, some of the birds in the field on the first visit may not be in the field on the second visit (or vice versa). The gist is that some of the variation between monday and wednesday's counts relate to detection (informed by the distribution of observed distances across monday and wednesday and perhaps substantial changes in the distribution of observed distances between monday and wednesday), and some of the variation relates to how many birds were actually sitting in the field (or sitting in the field and singing) on monday vs. wednesday. The phi formula is used to specify whether one thinks the number of birds that could be detected--because they are sitting in the field, or sitting in the field and singing--when the field is visited has some constant average value, or whether that average changes based on, say, whether it is raining or not, etc.

John

Ok, follow-up. This is a tough place for broad questions about how to analyze the data--pry better for specific coding or formatting questions--just because these questions take a lot of energy to answer and because online boards are probably not a great venue for teaching. That said, here's the best quick description of the models I can give, and hopefully you can work out a plan of attack with advisor, committee member, etc.

[for data formatting, etc., https://www.montana.edu/screel/teaching/bioe-440r-521/bioe-440-distance-sampling.html and https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/unmarked/vignettes/distsamp.pdf provide good overviews--and there are pry others if you search around on google.]

The three distance sampling options in unmarked are distsamp, gdistsamp, distsampOpen:

1) The closed distance sampling model (distsamp) estimates parameters that describe the expected abundance (lambda) and probability of detecting a given bird (sigma, via pformula). All parameters here and elsewhere could be estimated as varying in relation to covariates. Typically, distsamp is used to analyze data at a number of sites only visited once.With the data you have now, you could fit one of these models by 'stacking' the data (structuring the data so that each site*visit is treated as a different 'site', and adding a covariate for visit and/or year). This ignores any correlation between counts during different visits to the same site), and so to properly report the uncertainty may require some tricks after the fact (namely, a non parametric bootstrap). Ideally, average density = lambda/area. However, if some birds are not available for detection for behavioral reasons (see below), then this is really the density of 'available' birds. The formatting here for your y data as of now would be nsites*2 rows, and ndistance bins columns.

2) gdistsamp fits a model that estimates parameters associated with the expected number of birds that might have been available for detection (lambda), the probability that each bird that might have been available to detect was available to detect during time/visit t (phi), and the probability that any available bird was detected (sigma). Lack of availability might relate to not being physically present at a site during a given time, or might relate to a bird behaving such that it is essentially undetectable. If lack of availability is exclusively related to not being physically present, average density = lambda*phi/area. If lack of availability is exclusively related to behavior, average density = lambda/area (unmarked can report this, but note that it may not be appropriate).Typically this model is used to analyze data at a number of sites that have been visited a few times during, say, the same year. As the total duration across the visits increases, lambda becomes a little more difficult to interpret biologically. The formatting here for your y data as of now would be nsites rows, and ndistance bins*2 columns--each new visit adds another ndistance bin columns.

3) distsampOpen fits a model that estimates parameters that describe the expected abundance (lambda) during time 1,  the probability of detecting a bird, and parameters that describe the *change* from N[i, t] to N[i, t+1]. Typically this model is used to analyze data at sites that have been visited once per time period (e.g., once a year; although varying intervals could potentially work), when one is interested in population dynamics (the parameters associated with a density-independent or density-dependent model for population growth, demographic parameters related to the number of animals that 'stay' in a site from t to t+1 and the number of animals that newly 'arrive' at a site in t+1). The formatting here for your y data as or now would be nsites rows, and ndistance bins*2 columns--each new visit adds another ndistance bin columns.

'distsamp' is the most direct and simplest way to model 'just abundance'. It will be biased (as an estimator of actual abundance) if not all animals are available, and this motivated the development of the model underlying 'gdistsamp'. 'gdistsamp' will--*I think*--produce biased estimates of density if availability relates to both movement and behavior, and if individuals die or are recruited during the survey, gdistsamp is not robust to that, either (for multiple years, it might make sense to stack the data in so that a site is really a site*year). So really the choice depends upon what assumptions you think are reasonable, what you are trying to estimate, how you are willing to interpret it.

Your design is complicated. A big question is what constitutes a site. I don't know how to answer this because I have no idea how close the transects within the same field are, whether they are surveyed on the same day, etc. Are birds moving from transect to transect? If you survey both transect on a field on the same day or even exactly concurrently, could birds end up counted in both transect? I'd actually focus first on trying to figure out what defines a site, and then consider what design allows you to estimate the things of interest with the least headache. Three things to keep in mind. 1) dealing with the nesting here using random effects isn't possible in unmarked. 2) if you use the same design next year, it's also not possible to fit a model that estimates both availability and dynamics parameters in unmarked. If you used the same design next year, some sort of stacking seems necessary for either gdistamp (site by year ='site') or distsamp (site by year by visit ='site') to make much sense. 3) Although nobody likes doing it, very worst case scenario, a complicated design can always be simplified by throwing some data away (or better, with-holding some for out of sample model evaluation!). You could (for example) always sub-sample one transect and visit within each field and fit a model using, say, distsamp. You could fit the same model 4 times (one for each transect*visit replicate in a field) and, for peace of mind, check to see if the results are relatively stable, or if there's some pattern across time or transect that might inform how you sample next year.

John

Hi Katie,

1) Try using summary() on the output object. You should get a list with one element for the state model and one element for the detection model, and each should be a data frame containing the info you want. You can also extract the standard errors directly with SE().

2) Rota's paper used Bayesian approach and MCMC with Stan to estimate parameters. Unmarked uses maximum likelihood, which is usually much, much faster. The Bayesian approach has other advantages, for example, you can add random effects or customize the model structure (not possible in unmarked).

3) Missing values at some cameras is fine, as long as you are getting reasonable results don't worry about this warning.

4) This looks like a bug to me. I'll work on a fix. In the meantime, you should be able to make prediction work in this situation by fitting your initial model with the alternative approach to limiting interactions - set the formulas for parameters above order 2 to '0' or '~0'. So your stateformulas would be the 10 formulas you have now, plus 4 '0' s for the third-order interactions, plus 1 '0' for the fourth-order interaction (15). See the "fit3" example in the occuMulti help. Re-fit the model and then try predicting and it should work.

Ken

This is what occuMulti is doing behind the scenes, but it's obviously not working properly for predict at the moment.

Ken

melt(dataset, , id.vars = c("id_site", "date", "sampling spot"))

I know that it is difficult to evaluate my case without seeing my dataset but I am wondering if the structure of my data are not compatible with this pakage.

Obviously I tried to simplify and to run the models, and it worked.
For instance, I melted again the y dataframe, obtaining 10 rows as the siteCovs dataframe.
However, I wonder if this melting and melting makes my analysis poorer than if I would have used the 200 rows dataframe.
In fact, the resulting occupancy models are quite depressing.

Every suggestion is more than welcome,
thank you for your kind attention.
